preamble: Diphthongization of the high front vowel [i] (usually long [iː]) to [ei], the first step of a lowering path that often continues to [ai]. It occurred in Common Czech, where Old Czech ý, pronounced /iː/ by the 15th century, became ej (malý > malej 'small'), and in Cantonese, whose vernacular readings turn Middle Chinese -ij into -ei (四 sijH > sei3).

examples.note: Common Czech has the diphthong /ɛɪ̯/ (atlas ei) usually where Standard Czech has /iː/: malej, mlejn 'mill', plejtvat 'to waste', bejt 'to be'; a headstone of 1591 in Český Krumlov already spells it ey. In the 13th century the vowel of ý was /ɨː/ (malý /ˈmaɫɨː/); it merged with í /iː/ after consonant palatalization was lost, and that merger led to ý > ej.
The infinitive ending -ti was shortened to -t, as in Standard Czech být.
Vernacular reading; the rare literary reading si3 /siː³³/ preserves the monophthong.
Vernacular sei2 vs literary si2; also 地 MC dijH > dei6 /tei̯²²/ 'ground'.
